parts.text:
A curve has equation $y = \mathrm{e}^{x} - x^{3}$. One of its stationary points has $x$-coordinate $\alpha$, where $0 < \alpha < 2$, and $\alpha$ is a root of $x = \dfrac{\mathrm{e}^{x/2}}{\sqrt{3}}$.

A sequence is defined by $x_{n+1} = \dfrac{\mathrm{e}^{x_n/2}}{\sqrt{3}}$, starting from $x_1 = 1$. Find $x_2$, $x_3$ and $x_4$, writing each to 3 decimal places, and say whether these terms get closer to $\alpha$ from above or from below. (2)

mark_scheme.for: Puts $x_1 = 1$ into the formula to get $x_2 = \frac{\mathrm{e}^{0.5}}{\sqrt{3}}$, then feeds that value back in to get $x_3$
mark_scheme.notes: Evidence can be $x_2$ = awrt 0.95 or a correct numerical expression for $x_2$. Using a rounded $x_2$ to find $x_3$ is fine.

mark_scheme.for: $x_2 = 0.952$, $x_3 = 0.929$, $x_4 = 0.919$, all correct to 3 d.p., and says the terms decrease towards $\alpha$, so they approach it from above
mark_scheme.notes: cao for all three values. Needs the direction statement, e.g. 'decreasing, so approaching from above' or 'staircase coming down to $\alpha$'. Don't accept 'from below' or 'oscillating'.

solution.working: To 3 d.p.: $x_2 = 0.952$, $x_3 = 0.929$, $x_4 = 0.919$. Each term is smaller than the one before, and $\alpha \approx 0.910$, so the terms approach $\alpha$ from above. This makes a staircase that steps down to the root.

hints: Put $x_1 = 1$ into the right-hand side to get $x_2$. Keep the full calculator value (use ANS) when you work out the next term.
Look at whether each term is bigger or smaller than the one before it. That tells you which side of $\alpha$ they come from.

pitfalls.text: The terms $0.952, 0.929, 0.919$ all fall steadily, so they approach $\alpha$ from one side only. This is a staircase, not a cobweb. If you call it oscillating, or say the terms come from below, you lose the A1 even when your three values are right.

If you round $x_2$ to $0.95$ and keep rounding at every step, $x_4$ can drift away from $0.919$. Then you can't reliably tell how the terms are behaving, and a wrong value costs you the A1. Keep full calculator accuracy until the end.
